name: Pale Lilac
lede: Pale Lilac is a faint, greyed pink-purple, a color Ball uses to show how Rembrandt could make a violet tint without any blue.

sections.title: The name
sections.body:
Pale lilac is [[lilac]] with the strength turned down. Paterson uses the words to define lavender, "pale lilac" being his shorthand for the flower's color [1], and St Clair's glossary describes pearl as a very pale lilac-gray [2]. The swatch is a greyish one: ISCC-NBS block 252 calls it a "pale purplish pink", and Ridgway's 1912 atlas carries it [3]. The xkcd survey's version is more purple, #E4CBFF [3].

It sits with [[lavender]] and [[pale-purple]], and shades into the greys [1][3].

sections.title: Rembrandt's lilac
sections.body: Ball offers the best use of the phrase. Hendrickje Stoffels's dress in Rembrandt's portrait of about 1654 to 1656 might be called pale lilac, he says, yet it contains no blue pigment [4]. The violet tint comes from the faint blueness of lead white mixed with charcoal black, warmed with a little red lake [4]. It is a useful lesson: a color we name from a mix can come from pigments that contain none of its named hues [4].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: In our archive of 23,781 paintings, 41 carry this color over at least five per cent of the canvas, as photographed [5]. In 81 per cent of the 26 paintings where we measured its rank, it plays a light [5]. Sixteen of the matches are from the 1800s, and the earliest dated match is a painting by Bartolomeo Caporali of about 1452, a floor not a first [5].
